source.title: SGD Learns Over-parameterized Networks that Provably Generalize on Linearly Separable Data
source.authors: Alon Brutzkus; A. Globerson; Eran Malach; S. Shalev-Shwartz

record.tranche_reason: Tests width and generalization in an empirical natural-data setting, but does not run the random-label comparison or the original claim's experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper proves that sufficiently wide networks can represent arbitrary labels, but does not train them on random labels. Its MNIST experiment reports test generalization across widths; the exact figure values and width trend are not stated in the text. Results cited from other studies are not extracted.
record.test_reason: Figure 1 compares training and test performance across widths, bearing on V2 through a different activation and training setup. The supplied text establishes good generalization at all three widths but does not establish decreasing test error beyond interpolation.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. More precisely, with linearly separable data, Leaky ReLU, a fixed second layer and the specified initialization, the authors prove SGD convergence and a compression-based generalization bound independent of width. Their MNIST experiment illustrates good generalization across widths. Spurious local minima prevent extending their convergence analysis directly to ReLU; they do not conclude that ReLU networks fail to generalize.
record.recipe_differences: The empirical experiment uses a 3-versus-5 MNIST subset, Leaky ReLU, batch size 1, and trains only the first layer; the theoretical result assumes linearly separable data.
record.method_sensitivity: The experiment compares hidden-layer widths of 10, 100, and 1000; the latter two are described as over-parameterized.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 4 gives a network-size-independent upper bound on test error for linearly separable distributions under the specified Leaky ReLU setup and width-dependent initialization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SGD can have generalization guarantees independent of network width under these assumptions; this does not establish that widening lowers actual test error.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 8 shows that widening can improve the probability of reaching zero training loss on orthogonal inputs with ReLU.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Width can improve optimization success in this constructed setting; no held-out generalization comparison is provided.

record.problems: The empirical result is presented in a figure without numerical values or uncertainty in the supplied text. The data are a small linearly separable subset of MNIST, and only the first layer is trained.
record.rows_left_out: No other qualifying results were left out. The arbitrary-label expressivity theorem is a capacity result, not an observed training outcome.

untested.parts: No trained random-label versus natural-label comparison or random-label held-out accuracy.

Standard ReLU networks and downsampled CIFAR-10 are not tested; the experiment uses Leaky ReLU, binary MNIST and a fixed second layer. The post-interpolation test-error trend is measured in Figure 1 but cannot be read from the supplied text.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD comparison.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or generalization-gap ranking comparison.
No removal and retraining comparison based on example memorization.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict is justified from the available width results: R1–R3 do not reveal whether test error decreases, stays constant or increases. A width-independent upper bound is not evidence of a decreasing test-error trend. The arbitrary-label expressivity theorem, already declared in rows_left_out, does not demonstrate SGD fitting random labels.

versions.untested_parts: Does not train the same architectures and recipes on random labels and natural labels for comparison.

The experiment varies width and reports good generalization at each width, but the text does not state whether test error keeps decreasing beyond the width needed for zero training error; exact results are shown only in Figure 1.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
No sharpness or other generalization-measure comparison.

rows.subject: two-layer neural network with 10 hidden neurons
rows.operation_detail: Trained networks at three hidden-layer widths; compared training and test performance.

conditions.value: 4000 MNIST images, digits 3 and 5; 3000 training and 1000 test

rows.measure: Test generalization; exact test error not stated in text.
rows.note: Text says SGD reaches a global minimum and generalizes well in all settings; it does not specify this width's exact test error.
rows.check: The caption reports convergence and good generalization, but the supplied figure has no readable values. Neither the test-error comparison nor the interpolation threshold can be determined.

rows.subject: two-layer neural network with 100 hidden neurons
rows.operation_detail: Trained networks at three hidden-layer widths; compared training and test performance.

conditions.value: 4000 MNIST images, digits 3 and 5; 3000 training and 1000 test

rows.measure: Test generalization; exact test error not stated in text.
rows.note: The paper identifies this as an over-parameterized setting. Text says it generalizes well, without giving the test error or its change with width.
rows.check: The network is described as over-parameterized, but its test error relative to the narrower network is unavailable. Good generalization alone does not establish V2's decreasing-error trend.
